subtitle: Some questions no program can answer; others can be answered, but not quickly. And why every compiler is a pair of these machines.

ct.body:
What does “computable” even mean? The Church–Turing thesis gives the answer: anything computable by an algorithm is computable by a Turing machine. It cannot be proved, because “algorithm” is an informal word, but every model anyone has ever proposed agrees with it.

Then comes a stunning idea. A universal Turing machine takes the encoding of any machine M and an input w on its tape and simulates M on w. One machine that runs all machines! That is exactly the idea of the stored-program computer, the one on your desk. A universal Turing machine corresponds to a general-purpose computer running stored programs.
keynotes: The Church–Turing thesis: anything computable by an algorithm is computable by a Turing machine.
It cannot be proved because “algorithm” is informal, but every model proposed agrees.
A universal Turing machine takes the encoding of any machine M and an input w and simulates M on w: the idea of the stored-program computer.

halt.body:
Here is the most famous impossibility in computer science, and you can understand it in one sitting. Is there a program H(P, x) that always correctly says whether program P halts on input x? No. Let’s see why, by a trick of self-reference.

Suppose H existed and build D(P): run H(P, P); if H says “halts”, loop forever; otherwise halt. Now ask about D(D). If H(D, D) says it halts then D loops; if it says it loops then D halts. Either way H is wrong, a contradiction, by diagonalisation. So the halting problem is undecidable, and by reduction so are many others (does this program ever print “hello”? do two programs compute the same function?). What does it show? That there are well-defined questions no algorithm can answer.
keynotes: No program H(P, x) can always correctly say whether P halts on x.
Build D(P): run H(P, P); if it says halts, loop forever, otherwise halt; then H is wrong on D(D), a contradiction by diagonalisation.
So the halting problem is undecidable, and by reduction so are many others.

classes.body:
Some problems can be solved, but not before the sun burns out. To talk about how fast, we sort problems into classes. P is the set of problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic machine (sorting, shortest path). NP is the set whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time, equivalently solved in polynomial time by a nondeterministic machine: factoring, Hamiltonian cycle, SAT.

Clearly P ⊆ NP; whether P = NP is the most famous open problem in the field. A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time: solve one fast and you solve them all.

Feel the gap between checking and finding. Verifying a proposed Hamiltonian cycle in a graph of n vertices means checking each consecutive pair is an edge and every vertex appears once. That is O(n), polynomial, so the problem is in NP. Finding one by trying all orders takes up to n! steps. What is special about NP-complete problems? They are the hardest in NP; crack one and all fall.
keynotes: P is the set of problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic machine; NP is the set whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time.
P ⊆ NP, and whether P = NP is the most famous open problem.
A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time.
Checking a Hamiltonian cycle takes O(n), while searching all orders takes up to n! steps.

lex.body:
Here is where all this theory goes to work, in the program you use every day: the compiler. Its first phase, the lexical analyser, turns characters into tokens (identifiers, numbers, keywords). Each token class is a regular expression, and the scanner is a DFA built from them.

Look at the tiny DFA in the figure that recognises identifiers: a letter, then letters or digits. With l = letter and d = digit, the input “l d l” is an identifier. So which automaton underlies a lexical analyser? A finite automaton, a DFA.
keynotes: A compiler’s lexical analyser turns characters into tokens such as identifiers, numbers and keywords.
Each token class is a regular expression, and the scanner is a DFA built from them.
An identifier is a letter followed by letters or digits.

parse.body:
After the scanner comes the parser, and here we need the stack. The parser checks that the token stream fits the language’s context-free grammar and builds a parse tree. Top-down parsing (recursive descent, LL) expands from the start symbol. Bottom-up parsing (shift–reduce, LR) reduces the input back to the start symbol using a stack, which is a PDA.

Nested brackets and blocks need that stack, which is why a regular expression alone cannot parse a program. Try (a+a)*a: shift (, a, reduce a→F→T→E, shift +, a, reduce, reduce E+T→E, shift ), reduce (E)→F, and so on. Finally reduce T*F → T → E, and the whole input has become the start symbol E. Bottom-up parsing uses a stack to hold what has been read until a rule can reduce it.
keynotes: The parser checks that the token stream fits the context-free grammar and builds a parse tree.
Top-down parsing (recursive descent, LL) expands from the start symbol; bottom-up parsing (shift–reduce, LR) reduces the input back to the start symbol using a stack, a PDA.
Nested brackets and blocks need the stack, which is why a regular expression alone cannot parse a program.

summary.body:
Before you go: two lines to keep.

  • Halting is undecidable; some problems are solvable but not efficiently (NP-complete).
  • Compilers: lexer = DFA, parser = PDA/CFG.

Notice how neatly the whole course closes: the machines you studied are not museum pieces; they are inside the tools you use daily.
keynotes: Halting is undecidable, and some problems are solvable but not efficiently (NP-complete).
In compilers the lexer is a DFA and the parser is a PDA/CFG.
